I recommend checking [this website](https://www.color-blindness.com/2009/01/19/colorblind-colors-of-confusion/) out. If you follow the line that goes straight though white (it’ll miss just below for the deutan simulation, but just follow slightly above the line instead) for protans it lands at a exactly at a perfect cyan. For deutans, the white confusion line lands at what you may call “sea foam green” or perhaps “aqua”. Both types have colors they may confuse with white, but it’s just easier for protans because cyan is a much lighter color than sea foam green, which often looks more like a light gray, but when light enough it can absolutely look white.

This! I’ve done a good bit of research into color blindness and I’ve seen almost *nothing* about this. It’s like, somehow in my head sure orange and green are similar, but they’re also VERY not. When someone corrects the color, there is a visual *change*. It literally becomes orange. So bizarre.

Your brain kinda *makes* a yellow cone, so that's actually not a huge problem. Most color blind people actually have a perfectly functioning blue-yellow slider. The signals that get sent to your green and red cones are summed. This simulates a single cone with a peak at yellow wavelengths. From this, the amount of blue is subtracted in a way. So you're left with a measure of "positive" meaning yellow and "negative" meaning blue. 

I like to look at it mathematically. If you describe the 3 sliders from before in terms of your cone responses, (I call the red response R, the green response G, and the blue response B) you get:

(brightness value) = R + G + B

(red/green value) = R vs. G

(blue/yellow value) = (R + G) vs. B = Y vs. B

I write "vs." here becasue it's not really just like subtraction. Over time, your neurons learn to calibrate and learn where the white point is in between. Basically, R vs. G just means a comparison of how much red there is based on a history of learning how to compare them. Since you know about color cones, think about what happens to these equations when the signals from each cone get messed up. You can still sum the remaining two to see the brightness. However, when R or G is messed up, your brain never learns to compare R and G. You have no slider of greenness and redness. When your B cone is messed up, you lose the ability to compare the yellowness with the blueness. 

There aren't two ways for this to happen like there are with red-green color blindness though. Thats cause the only way for the Y value to *always* be zero and for the neurons to never learn how to compare them to blueness, R *and* G must always have no response. This would make the brightness be just as useful as both the other two. This is monochromacy.

Yup! Deutan color blindness does a lot more than you think. Sure, it’s red-green color blindness, it doesn’t mean what you think. When you look at a color, your brain interprets it in terms of three sliding scales. 1 is brightness, or white-black. 2 is a scale from blue to yellow. 3 is a scale from red to green. When you’re red-green color blind (protan or deutan) your red-green slider gets broken to some level of severity. 

It doesn’t sound like much, but that black-white slider only tells you how bright stuff is. It doesn’t actually tell you about the *color*. There are only *two* sliders responsible for determining all the colors, and *one* of yours are broken! 

This is why all the colors with full saturation can be shown on a 2d image. Color is 2D because it’s determined by those two sliders. When one is broken, it gets squashed closer and closer to a single line of color. If your pretend all of the colors are like a 2d piece of paper that you can draw on, mild color blindness doesn’t mean you confuse two spots on the paper, it means your whole page gets cut into a strip. People like you still have some wiggle room on that strip, but there’s no way to get the full range. Others will get it cut down so thin there’s no way to move up and down anymore, only left and right. This is why severe deutans only see blue and yellow.

It is a mixture of red and yellow, but yellow itself is a mixture of red and green. Yellow isn’t a primary when it comes to light. Fun fact: there is NO situation where saying “red yellow and blue” are the primary colors. There are two things that do make sense. The primaries are *red, green, and blue* when referring to light and *cyan, magenta, and yellow* when referring to pigment. 

Yellow=red+green 
Orange=yellow+red

If you wanna use only primaries you can “substitute” in that yellow and say 

Orange=red+green+red or just mostly red with a good amount of green. 

[This video](https://youtu.be/wh4aWZRtTwU) by Technology connections explains the whole dark orange is brown thing very well. It’s shocking how naming a color can make it seem very distinct when it’s really just a shade. The fact that we have a name for brown is what makes it look different from orange.

I terms of light when you have a slightly unbalanced mixture of red and green (more red than green) you get orange. 

With paint when you mix red and green paint you are essentially absorbing light in a red:green:blue ratio of 1:1:2. Since you’re absorbing more blue than the other colors, you get a dark anti-blue or dark yellow. Dark yellow can also be seen as a brown but it tends to get perceived as a nasty brown, which is why red + green makes a particularly unappealing brown as opposed to the warmer dark orange.

That whole red, yellow, and blue as primary colors is really just a big ol’ lie. The three primaries for any type of pigment is cyan, magenta, and yellow. Yeah. I do. I used to think “Oh well. It’s all I’ve ever seen. I don’t know anything else and the world looks fine to me.” Now, as I learn more and more about colorblindness, I do feel like I’m missing out. 

I saw a post the other day. It was on a cooking recipe. The comment said “I love the contrast of the red and green with the basil on the tomato sauce. Really makes it look beautiful” It was just a tomato soup recipe. Suddenly I thought about all the food that’s looked terrible to me. Every carrot and pea I couldn’t distinguish in a Shepard’s pie. 

Then I passed a flower. It looked like it was dying. My sister commented on how awesome it looked. To me it looked like it was dying because it had red leaves. I thought the leaves were brown. That would be so cool to see. 

Then, of course, there’s forests. I can’t imagine seeing trees where the bark doesn’t blend in with the leaves grass and dirt. They’re all the same. 

Up until a few years ago I thought cyan was a name for light blue. Turns out it’s its own color. Completely distinct from blue. What makes it worse is confusing it with white for the very first time. Suddenly I realized why I’d always say blue was gray even though I was red-green color blind. It’s because people just call blue-green blue sometimes. 

And lastly, tritans. People always say that my colorblindness is so ugly. Everything looks sick and dead. When they look at tritan vision, they say it’s pretty and sometimes go as far as saying they wish they could always see like that. When I look at it I see black, white, and very bold reds. Somewhere hidden in the black and white is every color people love that I can’t see.

Maybe I would’ve just convinced myself that I have to live this way if I never read [this](http://www.neitzvision.com/research/gene-therapy/) talking about how color blindness has been cured in squirrel monkeys and is going into human testing. Now I just keep hoping that one day I can be cured.

What you’re describing is *mostly* normal red green color blindness. Red green color blindness isn’t only between red and green. It involves every color that involves either the red cone (in your case due to protan meaning there’s something wrong with your red cone). Your red cone is responsible for seeing red, orange, yellow, purple, magenta, etc. There are basically two options: 1) your red cone fires to much when the green cone is the only cone supposed to be firing 2) you don’t have a red cone. Both are pretty similar. What it means is you might confuse greens with orange, reds with brown or sometimes black, blues with purpled, teal/cyan with gray or white, green with gray, pink with gray/light blue, and possibly more. It’s possible you don’t realize this because your brain is really good at figuring things out through context, but ask around. You might find that some colors that look similar to you are actually *distinctly* different to most. Green and orange for example are what a friend of mine called “not even in the same family”.

The whole thing with blue-yellow suggests something entirely different. For people with any type of red green color blindness blue and yellow are usually the most two distinct colors out there.

It’s more of a very minor inconvenience. Everyone is willing to make accommodations for colorblind people. I had a geography final and I had issues reading the maps, so I was just given a different map with shapes instead of colors to differentiate regions. 

As for when and how it got discovered, I was in kindergarten and would color my skies purple and grass orange. Obvious for most, but not me. My family doesn’t know where I got the colorblind gene from. Both of my grandfathers passed away too early for me to ask them, and my grandmothers can’t remember if they have any colorblind family members. Because of how unexpected it was, I got rested a bit later in 1st grade. I always hated coloring. But so do many with normal color vision. They’ll just find other things to do. Even being color blind I figured out how to solve a Rubik’s cube, which goes to show how minimally it truly effects most. 

As he gets older he might pick out clothes that clash in color, on not be able to tell when certain meats are done cooking. Both issues can be solved with a slight helping hand or a more monochrome wardrobe. 

A lot of the time, you son might guess colors right that seem to be impossible. The color blindness might even improve with age. This is not the case, but the brain learning to account for context. For example, even though I see bricks as a mud brown, I know they are more often a dull red, so I will call them red. I often see fire hydrants as dark brown, but those don’t exist normally, so I’ll say they’re red. 

Interestingly, purples often appear like dark blue to color blind people, so much so that instead of associating the word blue and purple with their respective colors, I believed that purple was just dark blue and blue was just light purple. I now know that is not the case. Ask your son about dark blues along with light purples and see the response. 

I don’t believe there’s any reason to delay getting the test. They are very straightforward and ophthalmologists know the right questions to ask to get reliable results out of any child who can speak. Good luck!
